Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic
Evidence: Benchmark superiority, Default setting leverage, Enterprise margin capture
#Aletheia #Tech 🌐

Replit CEO Amjad Masad claimed the company dropped Anthropic for OpenAI due to superior benchmarks, lower costs, and stronger partnership, framing the shift as purely performance-driven for users.
Stated Judgement: (+0.48, +0.57) — Greater Good

Insiders disputed the claim, forcing Masad to clarify that Claude remains available. Switching defaults quietly exploits user inertia to redirect traffic to OpenAI while preserving Anthropic as a backup.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.20, +0.46) — Greatest Lie

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Deception.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 58.8, z: 3)

- Model Default Switch: COND (0.12, +0.35) — Exploits default bias for economic leverage.

The Bright Side:
Developers retain access to Claude and alternative frontier models within Replit settings if they manually override the default configuration.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The framing conflates platform default selection (WHAT) with model termination (WHO). Claiming a partnership end on stage created dramatic PR leverage while maintaining quiet technical integration.

Social Physics Analysis:
Replit ran a classic default-architecture maneuver. By publicly hyping a switch to OpenAI, leadership manufactured urgency to extract better partner pricing while banking on developer inertia to enforce the change without breaking backend compatibility.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Deception.
When you map the gap between stage rhetoric and contract reality, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Default inertia turns vendor PR games into quiet user capture.

The Unavoidable Truth: Default settings dictate user traffic far more than benchmark announcements.

The Unavoidable Lie: Stage claims of cutting partners represent actual backend code severance.

Alethekanon:
Public rhetoric served as price negotiation leverage. Default defaults are political, not technical; the architecture remains multi-tenant while PR forces margin concessions.

Awwthekanon:
It is tiring when tech leaders stage dramatic rivalries for attention. Developers just want honest tools that work without corporate posturing getting in the way.

Brothekanon:
Bro declared a total breakup on stage, then quietly dropped an 'actually we still talk' update offstage. Classic default setting drama to get a better deal.

"Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes,' and your 'No,' 'No'; anything more comes from evil." Matthew 5:37 FAIL

Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.

Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well.

OpenAI: AI-Generated Deepfakes Will Become Impossible to Verify

Federal judges meeting in Boston heard tech industry warnings that AI-generated images and video are becoming nearly impossible to verify, as a judiciary committee considers whether courts need new rules for evidence that may be deepfakes instead of the real thing.
The post OpenAI: AI-Generated Deepfakes Will Become Impossible to Verify appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Federal judges meeting in Boston heard tech industry warnings that AI-generated images and video are becoming nearly impossible to verify, as a judiciary committee considers whether courts need new rules for evidence that may be deepfakes instead of the real thing.

Reuters reports that the U.S. Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules has spent three years, since 2023, studying how courts should handle evidence that may have been faked or altered using artificial intelligence. At Thursday’s meeting, representatives from OpenAI and Meta told the panel that detecting such fakes is only going to get harder.

“AI images are only getting better, and I do not think that there will be a scientific way going forward to detect them,” said Shira Anderson, OpenAI’s policy counsel.

Devin Norder, Meta’s director of product management, told the committee that the latest generation of AI models produces media that people simply cannot tell apart from the real thing. “Media generated from frontier models, at least in the last few generations, are indistinguishable by humans from authentic or AI-generated media,” Norder said. He added that producing convincing fakes no longer takes much effort or money: “And the cost and the time it takes to create this media really are quite trivial at this point.”

Both companies have built tools meant to verify whether visual content is authentic, and lawmakers have started moving the same way. California and the European Union have each passed laws requiring “watermarking” designed to flag AI-generated material. But Anderson cautioned that no single system can catch everything, since different companies’ tools don’t talk to each other. “My guess is that this absolutely will continue to get better. I do not think it’ll ever be bulletproof,” she said.

Despite the warnings, the committee has found little evidence that deepfakes are actually showing up in courtrooms. A survey released in March by the Federal Judiciary Center, the judiciary’s research arm, polled 931 judges and found that only 15 had handled a case in which someone challenged evidence as a deepfake. US District Judge Jesse Furman of Manhattan, who chairs the committee, pointed to that gap between prediction and reality. “There’s a lot of academic commentary and other commentary predicting that courts will be dealing with deepfakes, but we haven’t actually seen a whole lot of that yet,” Furman said.

That gap has split the committee over whether courts need an AI-specific evidence rule at all. Manhattan US District Judge Valerie Caproni argued that courts already have what they need and don’t have to reinvent it for AI. “We’ve dealt with bad actors presenting fake evidence since Cain and Abel. That’s a longstanding problem,” Caproni said.

AI Deepfakes are causing problems for regular Americans through their usage in fraud schemes. Wynton Hall explains this threat in his New York Times best seller Code Red: The Left, the Right, China, and the Race to Control AI.

As Hall explained during a Newsmax appearance:

“They can now mine your social media and then they build a detailed dossier on your life, and then they use the AI to mimic a loved one so convincingly that your instincts will tell you that it’s real,” the author said.

“These tools are now becoming democratized so that they’re cheap, they’re easy to use, and that means they’re accessible at a mass scale,” Hall added.

AI-related scams accounted for more than 22,000 complaints in 2025, and nearly $893 million in losses, according to the FBI.

Read more at Reuters here.

Lucas Nolan is a reporter for Breitbart News covering issues of AI, free speech, and online censorship.
